Morphing Wing: bending a trailing edge with one small servo

A student prototype testing whether a wing with a thickness provided 0.6 mm and nylon string can curve its trailing edge downward when a 9 g servo pulls the string. Modelled in SolidWorks. 

3D printed using bamboo lab 3D printer
0°

Illustrative model, not measured and not to scale. Amber line: nylon string along the lower surface. Blue block: servo inside the D-spar pocket.

Explore the buildBuild status

The problem, and what inspired us

A fixed wing has only one shape, so it is efficient for just one flight condition, and hinged flaps fix that only by adding gaps, hinges and extra parts. I am solving this by making the wing itself bend. My section is 249.7 mm long and 32 mm wide, with a hollow rear part whose thin skins, about 0.6 mm thick, act as the flexures. A single 9 g servo inside the D-spar pulls a nylon string tied to the tail wedge, which curves the trailing edge downward, and the thin skins spring it back when the string is released. 

ApproachPotential advantagesLimitations
Hinged flap and servoSimple, proven, easy to build.Gaps and a sharp change in shape; extra linkages.
Compliant morphing wingSmooth shape change; fewer moving parts.Needs careful flexure design; fatigue and stiffness must be checked.
This prototype3d printed wing driven by a string and a 9 g servo. Deflection, force, and repeatability must be measured.
I took inspiration from this video and made my own prototype - https://youtu.be/OKWurIhfkhQ?si=h4W3PRnrAXGuPUHC

How it is meant to work

The servo sits inside a rectangular pocket in the D-spar, the rounded nose of the wing. A nylon string is tied to the servo horn and runs along the lower side of the wing to the extruded part of the triangle at the trailing end. When the horn turns, it shortens the string path on the lower side and pulls the trailing end down. That's how the wing bends

Fig. 2 · Conceptual force path. Not measured.

Why the wing has give thickness 0.6mm ?

The reason behind doing this is because for 3d printing I have use PLA material which is a rigid filament. So to ensure it bends I had to give the minimal thickness so it works properly and also it doesn't break

Testing plan

video of testing - Morphing wing

Trailing-edge deflection

Photograph the side view against a grid at several servo angles. Measure the trailing-edge angle from the images.

Repeatability

Cycle the servo several times to the same angle and record whether the shape returns.

Servo load and current

Check whether the 9 g servo can pull the string through the full range without stalling.

Durability

Count cycles until any flexure cracks, and note where.

Method. Keep camera position, lighting and servo speed the same for each run. 

Safety and maintenance

  • Keep fingers clear of the servo horn and string while powered.
  • Ensure all jumper wire go correctly in Arduino so that Arduino remains unharmed.
  • Secure and insulate all wiring; keep the supply current-limited.
  • String should be placed perfectly to a angle so that it doesn't snap

Build status

Every stage of the build is complete: the wing was modelled, printed, assembled, wired and tested. The summary below shows the stages in order, with what was done at each one and the idea behind it.

CAD modelledServo pocket cut in modelThin-skin flexure designedPrintedAssembledTested

  1. CAD modelled

    Done

    What was done. The wing section was drawn in SolidWorks as a 249.7 mm long, 32 mm wide airfoil with a rounded D-spar nose and a hollow rear part ending in a flat tail wedge.

    The theory. A morphing wing has to be stiff where it carries the servo and soft where it has to bend. Deciding this in CAD first lets the nose stay solid while the rear part is made flexible, before any material is printed.

  2. Servo pocket cut in model

    Done

    What was done. A rectangular pocket was cut inside the D-spar, behind the nose cell, so the 9 g servo sits fully inside the wing with its horn on top.

    The theory. Keeping the actuator in the nose keeps the outer surface smooth and puts the weight near the front of the wing, away from the part that has to bend. The pocket also holds the servo in one fixed position, so the string always pulls from the same point.

  3. Thin-skin flexure designed

    Done

    What was done. The rear part of the wing was made hollow, with skins about 0.6 mm thick that act as the flexures. A hole in the tail wedge takes the nylon string.

    The theory. A thin plate bends easily because the force needed to bend it falls very quickly as it gets thinner. PLA is a rigid material, so a thick wall would not bend at all. The skins therefore had to be thin enough to bend, yet thick enough not to crack. The same elastic skins store energy while the string pulls and push the trailing edge back when the string is released, so no return spring is needed.

  4. Printed

    Done

    What was done. The wing was 3D printed in PLA on a Bambu Lab 3D printer, using the same dimensions as the SolidWorks model.

    The theory. Skins this thin are close to the smallest wall the printer can make well, so the printed part has to match the CAD closely. The printed layers also affect how the skin bends and how strong it is, which is one reason the result has to be tested and not just assumed from the model.

  5. Assembled

    Done

    What was done. The servo was fitted into its pocket, the horn was fixed on top, and the nylon string was tied to the horn and run along the lower side of the wing to the hole in the tail wedge. An Arduino UNO sits outside the wing and is connected to the servo with jumper wires. It powers the servo at 5 V, so no external power source is needed. The servo is controlled from the Arduino IDE.

    The theory. When the horn turns, the string path on the lower side gets shorter and the string pulls the trailing end down, so the thin skins curve. A servo is a good fit because it turns to a set angle and holds it, which makes the amount of bending controllable and repeatable.

  6. Tested

    Done

    What was done. The finished wing was run with the servo and a video of the test was recorded. It is linked in the Testing plan section.

    The theory. A morphing wing is only useful if it bends smoothly and returns to its original shape every time. Testing checks the bend of the trailing edge, whether the shape returns, whether the 9 g servo can pull the string through the whole range, and how long the thin skins last.

Scope of this page. This is a prototype built to test the idea. The video in the Testing plan section shows the wing working. Detailed measurements of the deflection angle and the pulling force are not reported on this page.
